title: Why a Swamp Cooler Makes Your House Dusty, and What to Clean
metaTitle: Why a Swamp Cooler Makes Your House Dusty | Las Cruces Cleaning
metaDescription: An evaporative cooler pulls outside air through a wet pad all summer, so the house breathes dust. What to clean, in what order, and what to leave to HVAC.
summary: Cooler season doubles the dust load in most houses here, and the fix is a different cleaning order.
transcript: An evaporative cooler works by pulling outside air through a wet pad and blowing it into the house. That's the whole design, and it's why it cools so cheaply in dry heat. It's also why the house gets dustier from May through September.

Two things ride in with that air. The first is whatever's blowing around outside, because a cooler is a one-pass system with a pad, not a sealed loop with a filter. The second is mineral carried off the pads themselves. Water evaporates, minerals stay, and some of that eventually goes airborne.

You also have to leave a window or a door cracked for a cooler to work. It pushes air in and that air has to go somewhere, so there's an outward flow running all day, and that flow keeps pulling new air and new dust through the building.

Start with the horizontal surfaces nearest the vents. Dust settles in a gradient, heaviest within a few feet of where the air lands. Wipe, don't dry-dust, or you'll put it straight back into the air. A barely damp microfiber picks it up and holds it.
Do the ceiling fan blades before the furniture, not after. Blades collect a thick felt of this stuff, and running the fan once you've finished the room redistributes all of it.
Window tracks and sills are the other place it piles up, because they sit right next to the opening the air is leaving through. A dry brush to loosen, then a damp cloth.
Floors last, always. Vacuum before you mop. On tile a mineral film builds that a dry mop slides right over, so use a damp mop and change the water as soon as it goes cloudy.

Fabric holds more of it than anything else. Curtains near an open window, upholstery under a vent, rugs in the path of the airflow. If the house feels dusty a day after you cleaned it, the soft surfaces are the reservoir you haven't emptied.

We don't service the cooler itself. Pads, pumps and bleed lines are HVAC work, and a unit on a roof is a fall hazard. If the dust is unusually heavy or the air smells musty, get the unit looked at, because a collapsed pad or a failed bleed-off throws far more mineral into the house than a healthy one.
localNote: Evaporative cooling is the default here for good reason. It works beautifully in low humidity and costs a fraction of refrigerated air. The tradeoff is that your house breathes outside air all summer, and outside air in the Mesilla Valley carries a lot of fine dust. Cleaning every two weeks through cooler season and stretching the interval in winter tracks the real load better than a flat schedule all year.

faq.q: Does a swamp cooler really make more dust than refrigerated air?
faq.a: Yes. Refrigerated air recirculates through a filter. A cooler brings outside air in continuously, and it has a pad, not a filter.

faq.q: Should I close the windows to stop the dust?
faq.a: No. A cooler needs an opening to push air out through. Close everything up and it stops cooling and starts pushing humidity back into the house.

faq.q: Why does the dust feel gritty?
faq.a: Some of it is mineral carried off the pads rather than ordinary household dust. It's heavier and more abrasive, which is also why it's worth wiping instead of dry dusting.

faq.q: How often should we clean during cooler season?
faq.a: Every two weeks keeps up with it in most houses. Once a month is usually behind by August.
